commons:508911.summary: A shepherd in a short red-brown tunic and leggings stands frontally with a sheep across his shoulders and a staff in his hand, flanked by sheep and goats among sprigs of greenery. Painted on the walls of a Roman catacomb, this pastoral figure was one of the earliest and most beloved ways Christians pictured Christ, who seeks the lost and carries them home.
facts: The Good Shepherd is the most frequently represented image of Christ in early Christian catacomb painting, borrowing the pre-Christian 'ram-bearer' (kriophoros) type.
The Catacombs of Domitilla, on the Via Ardeatina, are one of only a handful of Roman catacombs open to the public.
commons:508911.notes: Commons description is internally inconsistent (says 'circa 350' but dates the file '200–300 CE'); identification as Domitilla rests on the Commons category and a Belmont University web source, not on a museum record. Date given broadly.

cur:manuscripts-otto-iii-prayer-book-maj.summary: On the left page a figure lies prostrate before a domed church building; on the facing page Christ sits enthroned on a rainbow within a glowing mandorla, holding a book and blessing, borne up by two angels against a red, star-strewn ground. The double opening turns the reader's prayer into an act of homage before the heavenly King.
facts: Made between 984 and 991 for the private use of the young King Otto III, this is the only surviving prayer book of an Ottonian king; it is tiny (15 × 12 cm), written in gold on painted purple, with five full-page miniatures.
German Wikipedia notes that fol. 21v, the back of the Majestas, is left blank.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Under an arch at the left, Christ, haloed, is embraced and kissed by Judas among the soldiers; at the right, a young man runs away across a green ground, leaving his garment behind in the hands of a pursuer. The verse below — 'they that did see me without fled from me' — is illustrated with the young man of Mark's Gospel who fled naked at Christ's arrest.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.
